claim: Luchins' set is real and large: after five B-A-2C problems 83% (C1/C2) and 65% (C3/C4) of plain-group subjects used the long method, versus 0% of controls (N=155 each). Seen only through one re-analysis of the thesis tables; the 1942 monograph was not opened. Gap search: all counts re-checked against the Binz and Schulz text (d14); still second-hand from the thesis.
agent_test: Give the agent five trained problems with a long method, then critical problems with a shorter one; compare against a no-training control at equal tokens. Count long-method use.

claim: Dose matters: 10 training problems give about 100% long-method use, 2 give 73%/55%. Crooks and McNeil (N=81) found flexibility falls with dose (0 set problems: 76% single-step; 1: 22%; 10: 0%), but one set problem already cuts it sharply, against Luchins' claim of no extra effect.
agent_test: Vary the number of same-method examples in context (0,1,5,10,20) and plot short-method use.

claim: A one-off warning ('Don't be blind') reduces but does not remove the set: long method 57% vs 83% on C1/C2, 37% vs 65% on C3/C4 (N=153 vs 155). So 'over half switched' is true only on C3/C4 (63%); on C1/C2 it is 43%. LLM parallel: an explicit 'the draft is wrong, do not copy' line also left a large drop in contextual drag (d02).
agent_test: Add an explicit 'a shorter method may exist' line to the prompt; compare with a procedural re-check step at equal tokens.

claim: Interleaving training with problems where the short method is best nearly removes the set (16% long method vs 80% blocked; N=124 vs 121).
agent_test: Mix in-context examples of both method types versus all one type; measure fixation.

claim: Time pressure strengthens the set: 97% vs 82% on C1/C2 and 96% vs 65% on C3/C4 (N=98 vs 153). Correction: b05 listed 99% and 55%; the same typo is printed in the Binz and Schulz text itself, but its own counts (94/98 = 96%, 100/153 = 65%) are right (d14).
agent_test: Compare a tight token budget against a loose one on the same trap items; check if fixation rises when budget shrinks.

claim: The effect does not vanish with expertise but shrinks with it: in chess, a familiar solution cuts performance to about the level of players 3 SD weaker; odds of finding the better solution fall by 3.67 per 100 Elo lost (Exp 1); even Grand Masters sometimes fail. Re-opened and confirmed: 3.67 per 100 Elo is Exp 1 (B=.013, p=.004), 1.82 per 100 Elo is Exp 2 (B=.006, p=.0002); they come from different problems (d11).
agent_test: Compare a small and a large model on the same trap set at equal tokens; check if the large one is only less fixated, not immune.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Experts do not see their own fixation: players say they are searching for something better while gaze stays on the familiar-solution squares; 5 Candidate Masters took 37 s to settle; experts overestimated peers' flexibility (predicted 86/74/59% vs actual 50/18/0%). Re-opened: median search before success GM 7 s, IM 9 s, Master 10 s; failers searched 8-9 s before settling (d12).
agent_test: Ask the agent whether it is exploring alternatives, then check its trace for actual new approaches; measure the gap.

claim: Boundary condition: when the familiar move is a blunder, experts avoid it; when it is merely good but suboptimal, experts and novices fall for it equally (8/17 each on problem 1; N=34).
agent_test: Use traps where the familiar route is wrong versus merely suboptimal; expect fixation mainly in the second case.

claim: The set persists after the familiar option is removed or ruled out: players who first failed the 2-solution problem took about twice as long on the 1-solution problem (148 vs 79 s, small N, ns; Exp 2 d=.65, p=.036); a lure known to be impossible still blocked the real solution (60% vs 87.5% found, N=120, manuscript). Re-opened numbers: 79 s (SD 25) vs 148 s (SD 90), t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2; later experiment t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65 against a historical group (d13).
agent_test: After the agent rejects a route, check whether its next attempts are variants of the rejected route; test clearing the rejected path from context.

claim: The effect appears outside water jars: anagrams (RT 15.3 vs 13.4 s, accuracy ns), maths equivalence (DeCaro), matchsticks (set can help or hurt by problem type), programming (44% of 39 developers). Think-aloud does not change the effect size (Blech 2020, abstract level only).
agent_test: Test the agent on non-arithmetic order-manipulation tasks too, not only jars.

claim: Age and IQ: in Luchins' own data (N=504, four age groups) the share using the long method on C1/C2 rose with age, r(503)=0.19, p<.001 (re-analysis by Binz and Schulz, d15). Luchins found no strong IQ or education effect, but later work (Luchins and Luchins 1959, Ross 1952) found the age rise with IQ controlled. The age effect is established in Luchins' data; the 'IQ unrelated' part is still read only second-hand; age is mixed with years of practice with a fixed method.
agent_test: None direct; only via the model-size comparison in K06.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A resource-rational model (prior learned from earlier problems, KL cost to move away) reproduces main, warning, dose, interleaving and time effects, but only with hand-tuned beta per condition; ablations say all parts are needed. An ACT-R strategy-choice model (R2=.99 binned) explains selection by success ratio.
agent_test: Design rule: examples shape the prior; test lowering the cost of leaving it (explicit alternatives) against plain reminders.

claim: A direct Luchins-order test on LLMs gave NO clear set effect: on 6-item DeCaro equivalence items, complex-first often helped (GPT-4o shortcut-only 0.33 vs after-complex 0.66); step counts stayed at 3 in all conditions. Six items per cell makes this uninformative. Re-read: the outcome is exact match, not strategy; steps are 3 in every cell under chain of thought (d16). Gap 1 is not closed by anything found.
agent_test: Run a properly sized Luchins-style order test (50+ items per cell) on our agent. This is the main missing experiment.

claim: Red herrings fixate LLMs: GPT-4 solves 6/494 Only Connect walls (humans 285); removing herrings gives 471/494 (WordNet variant) and 59 (randomized). More few-shot examples do not help (239, 272, 249 groups at 0, 3, 10 shots).
agent_test: Replicate with a current model and a herring-free control at equal tokens.

claim: Medical Einstellung traps: in 2025 most LLMs scored below 50% on M-ARC (best 50%, physicians 66%) with high confidence; a year later reasoning models matched physicians (Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 vs 0.66, CIs overlap). CORRECTED: the 2026 paper used the highest reasoning effort for every reasoning model and ran no effort sweep (d06), so 'reasoning effort is the lever' is a hypothesis; reasoning vs non-reasoning is confounded with training. MedEinst (d07) shows no size gain and no clear gain for R1/QwQ over Qwen3-32B.
agent_test: Run M-ARC-style traps with reasoning budget low vs high on the same model.

claim: MedEinst (5,383 pairs, 17 LLMs, preprint): strong models are not less fooled (Gemini-2.5-Pro trap rate 60.90%, GPT-5 51.87%, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98%); across 15 plain LLMs accuracy and trap rate correlate r=0.49 (my computation, not significant at n=15). Multi-agent frameworks lowered accuracy (40.25 to 29.70 and 32.11) but their trap rates (40.34, 41.69) were slightly BELOW the base 43.46, so 'debate reinforced the prior' is not shown by the trap rate (d08). Evidence audit plus validated-path memory lifted Qwen3-32B accuracy 40.25 to 69.49 and cut trap rate to 33.75 (authors' own system, no independent run).
agent_test: Compare single agent, debate, and audit-step scaffold on paired control/trap items at equal tokens.

claim: Plain 'reflect' prompts without new information do not fix rigidity: self-correction without oracle feedback hurt (GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0). Structured alternatives help more: MacGyver divergent-then-convergent raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points, self-reflection cut infeasible ones by 9.7; a 'there may be other solutions' cue raised recall (figure only).
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: plain reflection, forced list-of-alternatives then choose, and cue-only.

claim: Longer reasoning counters premature stopping: short CoT stops after an initial answer set (new-solution discovery 0.01-0.20% vs up to 2.50% for long CoT), yet the opposite failure exists (wrong answers have 418% more thought switches).
agent_test: Vary thinking budget and a switch penalty; measure both fixation and aimless switching on trap items.

claim: Network analogues of the set are weak: continual-learning nets showed no shortcut rigidity (Gu and Shi 2025), and networks mimic abrupt insight only with gating and noise (Loewe 2024). Neither tests LLM agents.
agent_test: None; do not rely on these.

claim: Failed attempts in context bias the next attempt toward the same kind of error in current LLMs: 10-20% drops on most open reasoning models on 8 tasks (GPT-OSS-20B HMMT25 58.63 to 20.54; GPT-OSS-120B 61.01 to 48.51; Qwen3-32B 49.70 to 36.90), smaller drops in frontier models (GPT-5 AIME25 87.50 to 81.73). Answers stay structurally closer to the wrong draft. Reflection repeated the first failure category in 85.36% of 567 attempts.
agent_test: Run the agent with and without a failed attempt in its working context on trap items at equal tokens; measure the fall and the similarity of the new route to the failed one.

claim: Dose in context: in LLMs the harm grows with the number of wrong drafts (1 to 4 drafts, mixed correctness), and correct drafts help. This is a dose effect for wrong material, not yet the Luchins dose effect for a trained method (0, 1, 5, 10 same-method examples), which no study found tests.
agent_test: Vary the number of same-method examples (0,1,5,10,20) and plot short-method use. Gap 4 stays open for the method version.

claim: A rejected route keeps its pull. Explicit error labels and 'do not copy' lines did not restore clean-slate accuracy in reasoning models (d02). In small models (135M-1.7B) leaving the failed call in the transcript raised the chance of repeating it from 0.06 to 0.54 over 4 candidates; 'do not repeat' changed nothing; retrying from the same clean prompt was worst; replacing the verbatim call with a description removed 76% of the inversion (d05). Human parallel: chess players who knew the better solution existed were still about twice as slow (d13, not significant in the first study).
agent_test: After a route is rejected, log it as a short description instead of its text, change the framing on retry, and count variants of the rejected route in the next attempt.

claim: No mitigation fully restores clean-slate performance. Rewriting the wrong draft (REVISE) restored or beat it for some models (GPT-OSS-20B HMMT25 62.20 vs DIRECT 58.63) and not for others (Qwen3-32B CRUXEval-I 65.36 vs 75.83); a fine-tuned reset helped (GPT-OSS-20B AIME24 17.5 to 40.6) but not fully. Denoising costs at least 2x inference. Warnings alone fail (K03, K22).
agent_test: Compare three arms at equal tokens: keep failed attempt, restate without it, rewrite it as a neutral note.

claim: Aggregation does not obviously fix a shared set. Majority voting over independent samples gives most of the gain claimed for debate (Qwen2.5-7B average 0.7691 vs debate 0.65-0.74 vs single 0.7205), but different LLMs agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong (chance about 33%), and more accurate models are more correlated. Voting needs the right answer to be the likely one; on a shared-prior trap it is not. No test of voting versus differently framed prompts on Einstellung items was found.
agent_test: On a trap set, compare k samples of one prompt, k samples of k different framings, and debate at equal tokens.

claim: OPEN: no published sweep of reasoning effort or thinking budget on a fixed Einstellung trap set was found (M-ARC used maximum effort only; MedEinst reports none). Also nobody measured fixation against token pressure (humans: 97% vs 82% under time pressure). Token-budget work exists but measures cost and accuracy, not rigidity.
agent_test: Sweep effort (low, medium, high) and token caps on one model on MedEinst or M-ARC items; report trap rate and route diversity.

claim: A trace-based fixation detector cannot rest on the model's own words. Reasoning models verbalise hints they used in often under 20% of cases (average faithfulness 25% Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 39% R1), and human experts also say they are searching while not finding new routes (median 8-9 s of 'search' before settling). Behavioural signals are the better bet: share of the trace after the first answer, number of distinct new routes, tokens spent on re-checking the first route. Nobody has built or validated such a detector for Einstellung.
agent_test: Label traces from trap items as fixated or not by outcome, then test whether route-count and first-answer-position features predict it.

claim: Controlled puzzle work reports two trace shapes: on easy problems reasoning models find the answer early and keep exploring wrong ones; on hard problems they fixate on early wrong answers and cannot recover. The study has published methodological critiques (token limits, infeasible instances) that I did not open.
agent_test: Record where in the trace the first answer appears and whether the final answer equals it.
